Parabolic-elliptic and indirect-direct simplifications in chemotaxis systems driven by indirect signalling

Le Trong Thanh Bui Note: thanhblt@ueh.edu.vn    Thi Kim Loan Huynh Note: loanhtk@tlu.edu.vn    Bao Quoc Tang Note: quoc.tang@uni-graz.at, baotangquoc@gmail.com    Bao-Ngoc Tran Note: bao-ngoc.tran@uni-graz.at, tranbaongoc@hcmuaf.edu.vn (corresponding author)
Abstract

Singular limits for the following indirect signalling chemotaxis system

{∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c)in ​Ω×(0,∞),ε​∂tc=Δ​c−c+win ​Ω×(0,∞),ε​∂tw=τ​Δ​w−w+nin ​Ω×(0,∞),∂νn=∂νc=∂νw=0,on ​∂Ω×(0,∞)\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}c=\Delta c-c+w&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}w=\tau\Delta w-w+n&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \partial_{\nu}n=\partial_{\nu}c=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty)\end{array}\right.

are investigated. More precisely, we study parabolic-elliptic simplification, or PES, ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+} with fixed τ>0\tau>0 up to the critical dimension N=4N=4, and indirect-direct simplification, or IDS, (ε,τ)→(0+,0+)(\varepsilon,\tau)\to(0^{+},0^{+}) up to the critical dimension N=2N=2. These are relevant in biological situations where the signalling process is on a much faster time scale compared to the species diffusion and all interactions. Showing singular limits in critical dimensions is challenging. To deal with the PES, we carefully combine the entropy function, an Adam-type inequality, the regularisation of slow evolution, and an energy equation method to obtain strong convergence in representative spaces. For the IDS, a bootstrap argument concerning the LpL^{p}-energy function is devised, which allows us to obtain suitable uniform bounds for the singular limits. Moreover, in both scenarios, we also present the convergence rates, where the effect of the initial layer and the convergence to the critical manifold are also revealed.

Keywords: Indirect signalling chemotaxis system, Fast signal diffusion limit, Parabolic-elliptic simplification, Indirect-direct simplification, Initial layers.

1 Introduction

The term chemotaxis has been widely used to describe the directed movement of a species responding to a stimulus, with numerous applications in bacterial aggregation [BB72, EO04], cell invasion [RCP11, BBTW15], food chains [TW22, RTY24], and other contexts. In mathematical modelling, it turns into cross-diffusive terms in parabolic-parabolic or parabolic-elliptic systems of PDEs. Recently, chemotaxis systems with indirect signalling mechanisms have gained a lot of attention, where a system may include one species and two signals, or two species and one signal. Besides the suggestion of better responses of a species to the environment, see e.g. [NHWS10], the differences between the direct and indirect signalling also raise many interesting analytical questions, regarding the global solvability and uniform boundedness [FS17, Ren22], infinite-time aggregation [TW17, TW25], large-time behaviours [ZNL19, LLH20], or singular limits [LX23, LS24].

Let Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}, 1≤N≤41\leq N\leq 4, be a bounded domain with sufficiently smooth boundary Γ:=∂Ω\Gamma:=\partial\Omega. In this work, we study the singular limits ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+} and (ε,τ)→(0+,0+)(\varepsilon,\tau)\to(0^{+},0^{+}) of the following indirect signalling chemotaxis system

{∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c)in ​Ω×(0,∞),ε​∂tc=Δ​c−c+win ​Ω×(0,∞),ε​∂tw=τ​Δ​w−w+nin ​Ω×(0,∞),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n&\hskip-8.5359pt=&\hskip-5.69046pt\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}c&\hskip-8.5359pt=&\hskip-5.69046pt\Delta c-c+w&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}w&\hskip-8.5359pt=&\hskip-5.69046pt\tau\Delta w-w+n&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\end{array}\right.

which is subjected to the no-flux boundary conditions

∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=∂w∂ν=0on ​Γ×(0,∞),\displaystyle\frac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\text{on }\Gamma\times(0,\infty), (1.4)

and the initial condition

(n,c,w)|t=0=(n0,c0,w0)on ​Ω,\displaystyle(n,c,w)|_{t=0}=(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0})\quad\text{on }\Omega, (1.5)

where n0,c0,w0n_{0},c_{0},w_{0} are given smooth data. This system has been studied in [STP13, LX23] to model the movement of Mountain Pine Beetles in a forest habitat Ω\Omega, with ε>0\varepsilon>0 and τ=0\tau=0, where nn and ww represent the densities of the flying and nesting species, and cc is the concentration of beetle pheromones. In [FS17], the authors studied System (1), with ε=τ=1\varepsilon=\tau=1, which models the aggregation phenomena of microglia cells in the Alzheimer disease, where nn represents a species density and c,wc,w are the concentrations of two different chemicals. A variant of (1) with the setting in the whole spatial domain ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} can be found in [HL25]. For related models concerning indirect signalling, we refer the reader to [TW17, ZNL19, LLH20, Ren22, LS24, TW25] and references therein.

Biologically, signals can diffuse on a much faster time scale than the species self-diffusion, which leads to mathematical models that include a sufficiently small parameter 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1 appearing in front of the time evolution of the signal concentration (i.e., its time derivatives). This scenario has been discussed for the last several decades, where parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis systems had been simplified to their parabolic-elliptic relatives [CPZ04, KNRY22]. This type of simplification is well-known as the notion of fast signal diffusion limits or parabolic-elliptic simplification (PES for short) [WWX19, RTY24], which offers significant benefits not only in mathematical analysis but also in computational simulations. A PES is formally achieved by removing the signal evolution from the considered chemotaxis models, or equivalently, by formally assigning ε=0\varepsilon=0, leading to an elliptic instead of a parabolic equation for the chemical/signal concentration. However, rigorous analysis of PES has only been conducted in recent works, such as [Miz18, Miz19, Fre20, WWX19, OS23, RTY24]. On the other hand, by setting ε=τ=0\varepsilon=\tau=0, we see from the third equation of (1) that c≡wc\equiv w, i.e. the two signals coincide, and (1) is reduced to a chemotaxis system with a direct signal. Thus, the singular limit problem (ε,τ)→(0+,0+)(\varepsilon,\tau)\to(0^{+},0^{+}) is called indirect-direct simplification (IDS for short), and has also been considered for related problems in e.g. [LX23, LS24].

The main goals of this work are to study PES and IDS for (1) up to the critical dimensions, N=4N=4 and N=2N=2, respectively, where we prove the convergence and estimate the convergence rates including the initial layer effect. In the following, we first give the state of the art, which helps to highlight the motivation and novelty of our work. Then, we present our main results as well as the key ideas.

1.1 State of the art

The study of PES has been initiated in recent years, with the first work focusing on the classical parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel model

{∂tuλ=Δuλ−χ∇⋅(uλ∇vλ)in ​Ω×(0,∞),λ​∂tvλ=Δ​vλ−vλ+uλin ​Ω×(0,∞),(uλ,vλ)|t=0=(u0,v0)on ​Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\partial_{t}u_{\lambda}=\Delta u_{\lambda}-\chi\nabla\cdot(u_{\lambda}\nabla v_{\lambda})&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \lambda\partial_{t}v_{\lambda}=\Delta v_{\lambda}-v_{\lambda}+u_{\lambda}&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ (u_{\lambda},v_{\lambda})|_{t=0}=(u_{0},v_{0})&\text{on }\Omega,\end{array}\right.

(subjected to the no-flux boundary conditions) and its parabolic-elliptic relative

{∂tu=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)in ​Ω×(0,∞),Δ​v−v+u=0in ​Ω×(0,∞),u|t=0=u0on ​Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \Delta v-v+u=0&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ u|_{t=0}=u_{0}&\text{on }\Omega.\end{array}\right.

In [Miz19], the author positively answered the question: Does the solution of (1.1) converge to that of (1.1) as λ→0\lambda\to 0? With sufficiently small and regular initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0}, the author showed for N≥2N\geq 2 that uλ→u​ in ​C𝗅𝗈𝖼​(Ω¯×[0,∞))u_{\lambda}\to u\text{ in }C_{\mathsf{loc}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)) and vλ→v​ in ​C𝗅𝗈𝖼​(Ω¯×(0,∞))∩L𝗅𝗈𝖼2​((0,∞),W1,2​(Ω))v_{\lambda}\to v\text{ in }C_{\mathsf{loc}}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))\cap L^{2}_{\mathsf{loc}}((0,\infty);W^{1,2}(\Omega)) as λ→0\lambda\to 0, where the limit (u,v)(u,v) is the classical solution of (1.1). When the chemotactic flux is of the form uλS(vλ)∇vλu_{\lambda}S(v_{\lambda})\nabla v_{\lambda} (instead of uλ∇vλu_{\lambda}\nabla v_{\lambda}), [Miz18] showed that for a sensitivity S∈C1+ϑ​((0,∞))S\in C^{1+\vartheta}((0,\infty)), ϑ∈(0,1)\vartheta\in(0,1), satisfying 0≤S⁡(v)≤χ​(a+v)−k0\leq S(v)\leq\chi(a+v)^{-k} for a≥0a\geq 0, k>1k>1, the above convergence holds provided χ<χ∗\chi<\chi_{*} for some χ∗>0\chi_{*}>0 depending on k,a,N,u0,v0k,a,N,u_{0},v_{0}. In [Fre20], the author investigated PES for (1.1) but with non-degenerate diffusion of porous medium type. For the whole domain setting Ω=ℝN\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{N}, we refer the reader, for instance, to [KO20, OS23]. This PES has also been investigated also in [WWX19] in the context of Keller-Segel-(Navier-)Stokes system

{∂tnε+uε⋅∇nε=Δ​nε−∇⋅(nε​S​(x,nε,cε)⋅∇cε)+f⁡(x,nε,cε),ε​∂tcε+uε⋅∇cε=Δ​cε−cε+nε,∂tuε+κ(uε⋅∇)uε=Δuε+∇Pε+nε∇ϕ,κ∈ℝ,∇⋅uε=0,(nε,cε,uε)|t=0=(n0,c0,u0),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\partial_{t}n_{\varepsilon}+u_{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla n_{\varepsilon}=\Delta n_{\varepsilon}-\nabla\cdot(n_{\varepsilon}S(x,n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon})\cdot\nabla c_{\varepsilon})+f(x,n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}),\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}c_{\varepsilon}+u_{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla c_{\varepsilon}=\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon},\\ \partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}+\kappa(u_{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla)u_{\varepsilon}=\Delta u_{\varepsilon}+\nabla P_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\nabla\phi,\;\kappa\in\mathbb{R},\hfill\nabla\cdot u_{\varepsilon}=0,\\ (n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},u_{\varepsilon})|_{t=0}=(n_{0},c_{0},u_{0}),\end{array}\right.

subjected ∂νnε=∂νcε=0\partial_{\nu}n_{\varepsilon}=\partial_{\nu}c_{\varepsilon}=0 and uε=0u_{\varepsilon}=0 on the boundary. It was (conditionally) shown therein that this system can be rigorously simplified to its relative

{∂tn+u⋅∇n=Δ​n−∇⋅(n​S​(x,n,c)⋅∇c)+f⁡(x,n,c),u⋅∇c=Δ​c−c+n,∂tu+κ(u⋅∇)u=Δu+∇P+n∇ϕ,∇⋅u=0,(n,u)|t=0=(n0,u0),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\partial_{t}n+u\cdot\nabla n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(nS(x,n,c)\cdot\nabla c)+f(x,n,c),\\ u\cdot\nabla c=\Delta c-c+n,\\ \partial_{t}u+\kappa(u\cdot\nabla)u=\Delta u+\nabla P+n\nabla\phi,\hfill\nabla\cdot u=0,\\ (n,u)|_{t=0}=(n_{0},u_{0}),\end{array}\right.

via the limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, provided the following uniform-in-ε\varepsilon boundedness of ∇cε\nabla c_{\varepsilon} and uεu_{\varepsilon}

supε>0(‖∇cε‖Lp​((0,T),Lq​(Ω))+‖uε‖L∞​((0,T),Lr​(Ω)))<∞,\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Big(\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}((0,T);L^{q}(\Omega))}+\|u_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{r}(\Omega))}\Big)<\infty,

for some p,q,rp,q,r such that 2<p≤∞2<p\leq\infty, q>Nq>N, r>max⁡{2;N}r>\max\{2;N\} such that 1p+N2​q<12\frac{1}{p}+\frac{N}{2q}<\frac{1}{2}. Related results can be found in [LX21, LXZ23, WHZ25].

Besides PES, the investigation of IDS has also attracted considerable attention recently. A first work in this direction seems to be [PW23], where the authors considered a phenotype-switching chemotaxis model, which represents an indirect signalling scheme, of the form

{∂tuγ=Δuγ−∇⋅(uγ∇vγ)−γuγ+γwγ,x∈Ω,∂tvγ=Δ​vγ−vγ+wγ,x∈Ω,∂twγ=Δ​wγ−γ​wγ+γ​uγ,x∈Ω,∂νuγ=∂νvγ=∂νwγ=0,x∈Γ.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u_{\gamma}=\Delta u_{\gamma}-\nabla\cdot(u_{\gamma}\nabla v_{\gamma})-\gamma u_{\gamma}+\gamma w_{\gamma},&x\in\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v_{\gamma}=\Delta v_{\gamma}-v_{\gamma}+w_{\gamma},&x\in\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}w_{\gamma}=\Delta w_{\gamma}-\gamma w_{\gamma}+\gamma u_{\gamma},&x\in\Omega,\\ \partial_{\nu}u_{\gamma}=\partial_{\nu}v_{\gamma}=\partial_{\nu}w_{\gamma}=0,&x\in\Gamma.\end{cases} (1.12)

As γ→∞\gamma\to\infty, one expects the limit (nγ:=uγ+wγ,vγ)→(n,v)(n_{\gamma}:=u_{\gamma}+w_{\gamma},v_{\gamma})\to(n,v) where the latter solves the classical Keller-Segel model with direct signalling

{∂tn=Δn−θ1+θ∇⋅(n∇v),x∈Ω,∂tv=Δ​v−v+n1+θ,x∈Ω,∂νn=∂νv=0,x∈Γ.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\nabla\cdot(n\nabla v),&x\in\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v=\Delta v-v+\frac{n}{1+\theta},&x\in\Omega,\\ \partial_{\nu}n=\partial_{\nu}v=0,&x\in\Gamma.\end{cases}

This convergence was partially shown in [PW23], and later fully proved in [LS24]. A similar problem was considered in [LX23], where the authors studied the following system

{∂tnε=Δnε−∇⋅(nε∇cε),ε1​∂tcε=Δ​cε−cε+wε,ε2​∂twε=−wε+nε,(nε,cε,wε)|t=0=(n0,c0,w0).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n_{\varepsilon}=\Delta n_{\varepsilon}-\nabla\cdot(n_{\varepsilon}\nabla c_{\varepsilon}),\\ \varepsilon_{1}\partial_{t}c_{\varepsilon}=\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon},\\ \varepsilon_{2}\partial_{t}w_{\varepsilon}=-w_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon},\\ (n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon})|_{t=0}=(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0}).\end{array}\right.

Under the assumption that the initial mass ∫Ωn0\int_{\Omega}n_{0} is sub-critical, i.e. smaller than 4​π4\pi, this system is shown to converge to either

{∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c),∂tc=Δ​c−c+w,(n,c)|t=0=(n0,c0), or {∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c),Δ​c−c+w=0,n|t=0=n0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c),\\ \partial_{t}c=\Delta c-c+w,\\ (n,c)|_{t=0}=(n_{0},c_{0}),\end{array}\right.\quad\text{ or }\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c),\\ \Delta c-c+w=0,\\ n|_{t=0}=n_{0},\end{array}\right.

corresponding to ε1=ε2→0\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{2}\to 0 or ε1=1\varepsilon_{1}=1, ε2→0\varepsilon_{2}\to 0, respectively.

It’s worthwhile to mention that the modelling and analysis of chemotaxis systems with indirect signalling of the type (1), both in the parabolic-parabolic and parabolic-elliptic settings, have been subjected to extensive investigation, see e.g. [AY21, FLT23, Lau18, STP13, WP98, Wu22] and references therein. Even the question of global existence can be challenging, especially in the critical dimension N=4N=4, see e.g. [FS17, HL25].

Our current work adequately contributes to this literature by investigating the PES and IDS for chemotaxis systems with indirect signalling (1)-(1.5) up to the critical dimensions N=4N=4 and N=2N=2, respectively. Furthermore, we also provide the convergence rates, which have been seemingly completely left out in the literature, and reveal the effect of the initial layer.

1.2 Main results, challenges and key ideas

Notations: We denote by LpL^{p}, Wk,pW^{k,p}, for 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and k≥0k\geq 0, the usual Lebesgue and Sobolev spaces. Moreover, a general constant CC is used for any positive constant that does not depend on spatial and temporal variables, all the unknowns, as well as the relaxation parameters ε,τ\varepsilon,\tau. This general constant can vary from line to line, or even within the same line. In case where a dependence is important, such as the dependence on a terminal time TT or the diffusion coefficient τ\tau, we will write CTC_{T} or CτC_{\tau}, etc. For 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty, we denote by ΩT:=Ω×(0,T)\Omega_{T}:=\Omega\times(0,T)

To study singular limits for (1), we impose the following assumption on initial data throughout this work.

Assumption 1.1.

The initial data (n0,c0,w0)∈C1​(Ω¯)×C2​(Ω¯)2(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0})\in C^{1}(\bar{\Omega})\times C^{2}(\bar{\Omega})^{2} is nonnegative and satisfied the compatible condition, i.e., ∂n0∂ν=∂c0∂ν=∂w0∂ν=0\frac{\partial n_{0}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial c_{0}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0 on the boundary Γ\Gamma.

Our first main results are about the PES from (1)-(1.5) to (1.2)-(1.17). Fix τ>0\tau>0 and denote by (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) the solution of (1) with respect to ε>0\varepsilon>0. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, we formally expect that (nε,cε,wε)→(n,c,w)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(n,c,w), and the limit vector (n,c,w)(n,c,w) solves the system

{∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c)in ​Ω×(0,∞),Δ​c−c+w=0in ​Ω×(0,∞),τ​Δ​w−w+n=0in ​Ω×(0,∞),∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=∂w∂ν=0on ​Γ×(0,∞),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \Delta c-c+w=0&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \tau\Delta w-w+n=0&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \dfrac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\dfrac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{on }\Gamma\times(0,\infty),\end{array}\right.

equipped with the initial value condition

n|t=0=n0on ​Ω.\displaystyle n|_{t=0}=n_{0}\quad\text{on }\Omega. (1.17)

One of the main challenges when connecting solutions of (1)-(1.5) and (1.2)-(1.17) or (1.2) is the different structures between the parabolicity and ellipticity and the initial layer, especially in the critical dimensions, N=4N=4 for PES and N=2N=2 for IDS, see [NSY97]. First, to pass to the limit in a strong sense, the slow evolution (i.e., the products of ε\varepsilon and the time derivatives of cε,wεc_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) make the Aubin-Lions lemma difficult to apply. For example, the LpL^{p} maximal regularity applied to the slow-evolution equation ε​∂tuε−d​Δ​uε+uε=f⁡(x,t)\varepsilon\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}-d\Delta u_{\varepsilon}+u_{\varepsilon}=f(x,t), associated with the no-flux boundary condition, reads as

supε>0(‖ε​∂tuε‖Lp​(Ω×(0,T))+‖Δ​uε‖Lp​(Ω×(0,T)))≤(εp)1p​‖u0‖W2,p​(Ω)+Cd,p​‖f‖Lp​(Ω×(0,T)),\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Big(\|\varepsilon\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega\times(0,T))}+\|\Delta u_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega\times(0,T))}\Big)\leq\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\|u_{0}\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}+C_{d,p}\|f\|_{L^{p}(\Omega\times(0,T))},

see [RTY24, Lemma 3.4], which do not directly give a uniform-in-ε\varepsilon boundedness for the time derivative ∂tuε\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon}. Obtaining strong convergence for the slow evolution is tricky and usually requires considerable effort, see e.g. [WWX19]. Second, for fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 and τ>0\tau>0, even the global solvability for the system (1)-(1.5) in the critical dimension N=4N=4 is difficult, see [FS17, Lau18]. Some steps in that proof, involving e.g. the use of the heat semigroup or testing the equations for cε,wεc_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon} by cε,−Δ​cε,wε,−Δ​wεc_{\varepsilon},-\Delta c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon},-\Delta w_{\varepsilon} heavily depend on ε\varepsilon, and therefore do not yield the required uniform-in-ε\varepsilon estimates. For instance, the Duhamel principle for the latter slow-evolution equation, represented via the Neumann heat semigroup, is written as

uε​(x,t)=e1ε​t​(d​Δ−I)​uε​(x,0)+1ε​∫0te1ε​(t−s)​(d​Δ−I)​f​(x,s)​𝑑s,\displaystyle u_{\varepsilon}(x,t)=e^{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}t(d\Delta-I)}u_{\varepsilon}(x,0)+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_{0}^{t}e^{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(t-s)(d\Delta-I)}f(x,s)ds,

which yields that a uniform-in-ε\varepsilon estimate can only be obtained if the regularity of ff is sufficiently regular, at least essentially bounded in time, which is not the case in our situation. Third, it has been numerically demonstrated in [RTY24] that initial data starting far away from the critical manifold 𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}} (see (1.31)) can lead to a significant loss of simplification accuracy. Hence, to achieve simplification accuracy, an analysis of the initial layer is required.

In order to rigorously justify this simplification, we exploit the multiple time scale Lyapunov function, see Lemma 2.2,

ℰ⁡(nε,cε):=∫Ω(nε​(log⁡nε−cε)+12​|Δ​cε−cε+wε|2+τ2​|Δ​cε|2+1+τ2​|∇cε|2+12​cε2),\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}):=\int_{\Omega}\left(n_{\varepsilon}(\log n_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon})+\frac{1}{2}|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\frac{\tau}{2}|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\frac{1+\tau}{2}|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{\varepsilon}^{2}\right), (1.18)

with its dissipation given by

𝒟⁡(nε,cε)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}) :=−dd​t​ℰ​(nε,cε)\displaystyle:={-\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon})} (1.19)
=∫Ω(nε​|∇(log⁡nε−cε)|2+1+τε​|∇(Δ​cε−cε+wε)|2+2ε​|Δ​cε−cε+wε|2).\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\Big(n_{\varepsilon}|\nabla(\log n_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon})|^{2}+\frac{1+\tau}{\varepsilon}|\nabla(\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon})|^{2}+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\Big).

It is remarked that the term nε​(log⁡nε−cε)n_{\varepsilon}(\log n_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}) in the Lyapunov function ℰ⁡(nε,cε)\mathcal{E}(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}) has no sign and needs to be estimated from below. If 1≤N≤31\leq N\leq 3, the Sobolev embedding is sufficient to absorb the norm of nε​cεn_{\varepsilon}c_{\varepsilon} in L∞​((0,T),L1​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{1}(\Omega)) into the L∞​((0,T),H2​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);H^{2}(\Omega))-norm of cεc_{\varepsilon} in ℰ⁡(nε,cε)\mathcal{E}(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}), cf. Lemma 2.3, and to obtain an L∞​(ΩT)L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})-estimate for nεn_{\varepsilon}. In the critical dimension N=4N=4, the method of using the Adam-type inequality, see [FS17, Section 7], can be adapted to balance the energy-dissipation equality. Unfortunately, because of the slow evolution, the locally spatial truncation argument in [FS17, Section 8] does not work to control the LpL^{p}-energy. We overcome this issue by adapting the idea of combining the Sobolev, Gagliardo-Nirenberg, and Young inequalities in [HL25, Proof of Theorem 1.2]. Then, some feedback arguments, using the heat semigroup as well as maximal regularity with slow evolution, help us to estimate the slow evolution’s components wε,cεw_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon}.

The strong convergence cε→cc_{\varepsilon}\to c in L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)) is challenging, see e.g. [WWX19, Section 5], where this was proved by heavily exploiting the higher regularity of cεc_{\varepsilon}. In this work, we provide a shortened and more direct proof by employing the argument from (2.33)-(2.37), which is basically based on the so-called energy equation method, see e.g. [Bal04, HT16]. This method uses the equation obtained by considering an L2L^{2} energy of (cε−c)(c_{\varepsilon}-c), instead of the energy inequality, and then shows the convergence in norms before using the uniform convexity of L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)) to get the strong convergence.

Theorem 1.1 (PES for (1)).

Let 1≤N≤41\leq N\leq 4 and fix τ>0\tau>0. Assume that (n0,c0,w0)(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0}) is complied with Assumption 1.1, and furthermore in the critical dimension N=4N=4 that Ω=BR\Omega=B_{R} for some R>0R>0 and

M:=∫Ωn0<64​τ​π2.\displaystyle M{:=\int_{\Omega}n_{0}}<64\tau\pi^{2}. (1.20)

For each ε>0\varepsilon>0, let (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) be the global classical solution to parabolic-parabolic system (1)-(1.5), given by Theorem 2.1. Then, for any 0<T<∞0<T<\infty,

supε>0(‖nε‖Cγ,γ/2​(Ω¯×[0,T])+‖nε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)))≤Cτ,T,supε>0(‖wε‖L∞​((0,T),W1,∞​(Ω))+‖Δ​wε‖Lp​(ΩT)+‖cε‖L∞​((0,T),W2,∞​(Ω)))≤Cτ,T,p,\displaystyle\begin{gathered}\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Big(\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{C^{\gamma,\gamma/2}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}\Big)\leq C_{\tau,T},\\ \sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Big(\|w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);W^{1,\infty}(\Omega))}+\|\Delta w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}+\|c_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);W^{2,\infty}(\Omega))}\Big)\leq C_{\tau,T,p},\end{gathered}

for some γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and any 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, we have the following limits

nε⟶nstrongly inC⁡(Ω¯×[0,T]),∇nε⇀∇nweakly inL2​(ΩT),cε⟶cstrongly inL2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)),wε⟶wstrongly inL2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \begin{array}[]{llllcl}n_{\varepsilon}&\longrightarrow&n&\text{strongly in}&C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]),\\ \nabla n_{\varepsilon}&\xrightharpoonup{\hskip 10.81218pt}&\nabla n&\text{weakly in}&L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),\\ c_{\varepsilon}&\longrightarrow&c&\text{strongly in}&L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)),\\ w_{\varepsilon}&\longrightarrow&w&\text{strongly in}&L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)),\end{array}\end{aligned} (1.23)

and the limit vector (n,c,w)(n,c,w) is the unique global classical solution to the indirect signalling parabolic-elliptic system (1.2)-(1.17).

As a by-product of the proof of Theorem 1.1, we have the following convergences, which also explain the mechanism of the PES

‖ε​∂tcε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))=‖Δ​cε−cε+wε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))≤Cτ​ε,\displaystyle\|\varepsilon\partial_{t}c_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}=\|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}\leq C_{\tau}\sqrt{\varepsilon}, (1.24)
ε​∂twε=τ​Δ​wε−wε+nε⇀0 in distributional sense.\displaystyle\varepsilon\partial_{t}w_{\varepsilon}=\tau\Delta w_{\varepsilon}-w_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\quad\xrightharpoonup{\hskip 10.81218pt}\quad 0\quad{\text{ in distributional sense}}.

Up to now, we have only obtained the weak convergence for the equation of wεw_{\varepsilon} due to a lack of uniform regularity information of ∂twε\partial_{t}w_{\varepsilon}. We show that this strong convergence will be a consequence of the next part, where the accuracy of the PES provided in Theorem 1.1 is investigated. By subtracting the corresponding equations of solution components of the systems (1)-(1.5) and (1.2)-(1.17), we see that the vector (n~ε,c~ε,w~ε):=(nε−n,cε−c,wε−w)(\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon},\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon},\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}):=(n_{\varepsilon}-n,c_{\varepsilon}-c,w_{\varepsilon}-w) is the solution of the so-called rate system

{∂tn~ε=Δn~ε−∇⋅(n~ε∇cε+n∇c~ε)in ​Ω∞,ε​∂tc~ε=Δ​c~ε−c~ε+w~ε−ε​∂tcin ​Ω∞,ε​∂tw~ε=τ​Δ​w~ε−w~ε+n~ε−ε​∂twin ​Ω∞,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}&\hskip-5.69046pt=&\Delta\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}-\nabla\cdot(\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}\nabla c_{\varepsilon}+n\nabla\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon})&\text{in }\Omega_{\infty},\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}&\hskip-5.69046pt=&\Delta\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}-\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}+\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon\partial_{t}c&\text{in }\Omega_{\infty},\\ \varepsilon\partial_{t}\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}&\hskip-5.69046pt=&\tau\Delta\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}-\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}+\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon\partial_{t}w&\text{in }\Omega_{\infty},\end{array}\right.

which is subjected to the boundary conditions

∂n~ε∂ν=∂c~ε∂ν=∂w~ε∂ν=0on ​Γ∞,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\text{on }\Gamma_{\infty}, (1.28)

and the initial value condition

(n~ε​(0),c~ε​(0),w~ε​(0))=(0,c0−c⁡(0),w0−w⁡(0)).\displaystyle(\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}(0),\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}(0),\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}(0))=(0,c_{0}-c(0),w_{0}-w(0)). (1.29)

It is obvious to see that c⁡(0)c(0) and w⁡(0)w(0) are not given a priori, and they may be well different from c0c_{0} and w0w_{0}, respectively. These missing initial values can only be recovered, thanks to the last two equations in (1.2)-(1.17), as

w⁡(x,0)=(−τ​Δ+I)−1​n0,c⁡(x,0)=(−Δ+I)−1​w​(x,0).\displaystyle w(x,0)=(-\tau\Delta+I)^{-1}n_{0},\quad c(x,0)=(-\Delta+I)^{-1}w(x,0). (1.30)

This difference in the initial values is referred to as the initial layer. It has been usually assumed to be zero in the literature, see e.g. [LX24]. However, this turns out to be important in studying the accuracy of the PES (or IDS), which is evidenced in the recent work [RTY24], where the effect of the initial layer has been carefully analysed for the PES of a competitive prey-predator chemotaxis system. This effect is especially relevant when the original initial data (n0,c0,w0)(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0}) do not lie on the critical manifold, which is defined by

𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲:={(n,c,w)∈L2​(Ω)×H2​(Ω)2:(Δ​c−c+w,τ​Δ​w−w+n)=(0,0)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}:=\Big\{(n,c,w)\in L^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{2}(\Omega)^{2}:\,(\Delta c-c+w,\,\tau\Delta w-w+n)=(0,0)\Big\}. (1.31)

We define the distance from the initial data (n0,c0,w0)(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0}) to the critical manifold 𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}} with respect to the topology Wk,p​(Ω)×Wl,p​(Ω)W^{k,p}(\Omega)\times W^{l,p}(\Omega) by

distpk,l​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲]:=‖−Δ​c0+c0−w0‖Wk,p​(Ω)2+‖−τ​Δ​w0+w0−n0‖Wl,p​(Ω)2,\displaystyle\mathrm{dist}^{k,l}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]:={\sqrt{\|-\Delta c_{0}+c_{0}-w_{0}\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|-\tau\Delta w_{0}+w_{0}-n_{0}\|_{W^{l,p}(\Omega)}^{2}}}\,, (1.32)

for k,l∈ℕk,l\in\mathbb{N} and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty. When k=l=0k=l=0, p=2p=2, we conveniently write dist:=dist20,0\mathrm{dist}:=\mathrm{dist}^{0,0}_{2}. By using the following representations of the inverse operators (−Δ+I)−1(-\Delta+I)^{-1} and (−τ​Δ+I)−1(-\tau\Delta+I)^{-1}, see e.g. [RTY24],

{c~ε​(x,0)=∫0∞es⁡(Δ−I)​[−Δ​c0​(x)+c0​(x)−w0​(x)]​ds,x∈Ω,w~ε​(x,0)=∫0∞es⁡(τ​Δ−I)​[−τ​Δ​w0​(x)+w0​(x)−n0​(x)]​ds,x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\displaystyle\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}(x,0)\;=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{s(\Delta-I)}[-\Delta c_{0}(x)+c_{0}(x)-w_{0}(x)]ds,&x\in\Omega,\\ \displaystyle\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}(x,0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{s(\tau\Delta-I)}[-\tau\Delta w_{0}(x)+w_{0}(x)-n_{0}(x)]ds,&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

we can estimate these the initial layers by the distance distp1,2​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲]\mathrm{dist}^{1,2}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}], see Lemma 3.1. Then, we can employ the uniform-in-ε\varepsilon estimates in Theorem 1.1 to obtain for each 1≤k∈ℕ1\leq k\in\mathbb{N} (see Lemma 3.3),

dd​t∫Ωn~ε2​k(t)≤−2​k−1k∫Ω|∇n~εk|2+Ck,T∫Ωn~ε2​k+Ck,T∫Ω|∇c~ε|2,\displaystyle\dfrac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}^{2k}(t)\leq-\dfrac{2k-1}{k}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}^{k}|^{2}+C_{k,T}\int_{\Omega}\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}^{2k}+C_{k,T}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}|^{2},

to test the equations for c~ε,w~ε\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon},\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}, and apply the fundamental differential inequality given in Lemma A.6 to obtain convergence rates as follows.

Theorem 1.2 (Convergence rates and the initial layer’s effect).

Let 1≤N≤41\leq N\leq 4, and fix τ>0\tau>0. For each ε>0\varepsilon>0, let (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) be the global classical solution to the system (1)-(1.5), given by Theorem 2.1.

(1.37)

and

‖w~ε‖Lp​((0,T),W2,p​(Ω))≤Cp,τ,T​(ε2p+ε1p​(distp0,2​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])2p),‖c~ε‖Lp​((0,T),W4,p​(Ω))≤Cp,τ,T​(ε2p+ε1p​(distp4,2​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])2p).\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lllll}\displaystyle\|\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}((0,T);W^{2,p}(\Omega))}&\hskip-5.69046pt\displaystyle\leq C_{p,\tau,T}\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{p}}+\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{p}}\big(\mathrm{dist}^{0,2}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)^{\frac{2}{p}}\right),\\ \displaystyle\|\widetilde{c}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}((0,T);W^{4,p}(\Omega))}&\hskip-5.69046pt\displaystyle\leq C_{p,\tau,T}\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{p}}+\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{p}}\big(\mathrm{dist}^{4,2}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)^{\frac{2}{p}}\right).\end{array}
Remark 1.1.
  • •

    In the above estimates, the general constants CT,τC_{T,\tau}, Cp,T,τC_{p,T,\tau} may tend to infinity as τ→0\tau\to 0.

  • •

    Thanks to the estimate (1.35), the rate ‖n~ε‖L∞​((0,T),L2​(Ω))\|\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega))} is of order O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) if the distance dist⁡[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲]\mathrm{dist}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}] is at least of the order ε\sqrt{\varepsilon}. Even if dist⁡[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲]\mathrm{dist}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}] is large (i.e., the system starts far away from the critical manifold 𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}), nεn_{\varepsilon} always converges to nn in L∞​((0,T),L2​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega)) at least in the order O⁡(ε)O(\sqrt{\varepsilon}). However, this is not true for cεc_{\varepsilon} and wεw_{\varepsilon}.

    In [RTY24], it has been shown numerically that, if a system starts far away from its critical manifold, then the slow evolution’s components do not converge to their expected limits in L∞​((0,T),L2​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega)), and, in contrast, the distances between the solutions can be even sufficiently large.

  • •

    Since the initial conditions are a major difference between the ε\varepsilon-dependent and limiting systems, a non-zero distance from the initial data to 𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}} corresponds to an initial layer. Therefore, Theorem 1.2 also claims that the parabolic-elliptic system (1.2)-(1.17) is a “good” approximation of the parabolic-parabolic system (1)-(1.5) whenever there is no initial layer, which is recently discussed in [LX24]. This suggests that skipping the slow time evolution should be associated with well-prepared initial data.

As discussed after Theorem (1.1), we see that the weak convergence in (1.24) can, in fact, be proved in the strong topology. The following corollary is understood as the strong convergence to the critical manifold CPESC_{\textsf{PES}}.

Corollary 1 (Strong convergence to the critical manifold).

For each ε>0\varepsilon>0, let (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) be the global classical solution to the system (1)-(1.5). Then it holds

‖Δ​cε−cε+wε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖τ​Δ​wε−wε+nε‖L2​(ΩT)≤CT,τ​ε.\displaystyle\|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|\tau\Delta w_{\varepsilon}-w_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C_{T,\tau}\sqrt{\varepsilon}. (1.41)

Furthermore, if dist20,1​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲]=O⁡(ε)\mathrm{dist}^{0,1}_{2}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]=O(\varepsilon) then we have the improved convergence rate

‖Δ​cε−cε+wε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖τ​Δ​wε−wε+nε‖L2​(ΩT)≤CT,τ​ε.{\|\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|\tau\Delta w_{\varepsilon}-w_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C_{T,\tau}{\varepsilon}.}
Proof.

By the triangle inequality and the fact that τ​Δ​w−w+n=0\tau\Delta w-w+n=0,

‖τ​Δ​wε−wε+nε‖L2​(ΩT)≤\displaystyle\|\tau\Delta w_{\varepsilon}-w_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq\, ‖τ​Δ​w~ε−w~ε+n~ε‖L2​(ΩT)\displaystyle\,{\|\tau\Delta\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}-\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}+\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}}
≤\displaystyle\leq\, τ​‖w~ε‖L2​(0,T,H2​(Ω))+‖w~ε‖L2​(ΩT)+‖n~ε‖L2​(ΩT)\displaystyle\,{\tau\|\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}(\Omega))}+\|\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\|\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}}
≤\displaystyle\leq\, CT,τ​(ε+ε​dist20,1​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])\displaystyle\,C_{T,\tau}\big(\varepsilon+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\mathrm{dist}^{0,1}_{2}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)

thanks to (1.38) and (1.2). The convergence for Δ​cε−cε+wε\Delta c_{\varepsilon}-c_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon} follows similarly. ∎

Our second main results concerning rigorous IDS for (1)-(1.5) will be presented in Theorem 1.3. More precisely, we study the limit as κ=(ε,τ)→(0,0)\kappa=(\varepsilon,\tau)\to(0,0), or in other words, both parameters ε\varepsilon and τ\tau tend to zero at the same time. Here, the subscript κ\kappa in (nκ,cκ,wκ)(n_{\kappa},c_{\kappa},w_{\kappa}) is used to indicate the dependence of the solution on both parameters. We formally expect

(nκ,cκ,wκ)→(n,c,w)​and​(ε​∂tcκ,ε​∂twκ−τ​Δ​wκ)=(Δ​cκ−cκ+wκ,−wκ+nκ)→(0,0),\displaystyle(n_{\kappa},c_{\kappa},w_{\kappa})\rightarrow(n,c,w)\;\text{and}\;(\varepsilon\partial_{t}c_{\kappa},\varepsilon\partial_{t}w_{\kappa}-\tau\Delta w_{\kappa})=(\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa},-w_{\kappa}+n_{\kappa})\rightarrow(0,0), (1.42)

and subsequently, at the limit level w=nw=n. Therefore, the vector (n,c)(n,c) is expected to be the solution to

{∂tn=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c)in ​Ω×(0,∞),Δ​c−c+n=0in ​Ω×(0,∞),∂n∂ν=∂c∂ν=0on ​Γ×(0,∞),n|t=0=n0on ​Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\partial_{t}n=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \Delta c-c+n=0&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \dfrac{\partial n}{\partial\nu}=\dfrac{\partial c}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{on }\Gamma\times(0,\infty),\\ n|_{t=0}=n_{0}&\text{on }\Omega,\end{array}\right.

which describes a direct signalling mechanism and is the well-known Keller-Segel system. Particularly, if τ=ε\tau=\varepsilon, or τ,ε\tau,\varepsilon are given in the same time scale, the equation for wεw_{\varepsilon} can be rewritten as

∂twε−Δ​wε=−1ε​(wε−nε)\displaystyle\partial_{t}w_{\varepsilon}-\Delta w_{\varepsilon}=-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(w_{\varepsilon}-n_{\varepsilon}\right)

in which the kinetics of wεw_{\varepsilon} is on a much faster time scale compared to its evolution and diffusion. The limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 then falls into the topic of fast reaction limits, which has usually been studied in reaction-diffusion systems with fast interaction, see e.g. [BPR12, PS23, TT24, MSTT24], and recently in chemotaxis systems [LS24, LX23]. To rigorously prove IDS, similarly to Theorem 1.1, it is important to control the Lyapunov functional ℰ⁡(nκ,cκ)\mathcal{E}(n_{\kappa},c_{\kappa}) as well as to obtain the uniform-in-κ\kappa estimates in L∞​(ΩT)L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T}), and therefore, we face similar challenges as in the first part. Furthermore, due to τ→0+\tau\to 0^{+}, the Lyapunov structure from Theorem 1.1 only gives the uniform-in-κ\kappa boundedness in L∞​((0,T),H1​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)) since the term of second order derivatives of cκc_{\kappa} now depends explicitly on κ\kappa. Obtaining uniform-in-κ\kappa estimates is quite tricky since now both ε\varepsilon and τ\tau can be degenerate. Our idea is to adapt the bootstrap argument proposed in [MSTT24]. The starting point in this argument is given in Lemma 4.3, where we show there is a small constant δ>0\delta>0 such that

supκ∈(0,∞)2(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκ1+δ2(t)+∥nκ∥L2+δ​(ΩT)+∬ΩTnκδ2−1|∇nκ|2)≤CT.\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{1+\frac{\delta}{2}}(t)+\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2+\delta}(\Omega_{T})}+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{\frac{\delta}{2}-1}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}\right)\leq C_{T}.

Then, based on a combination of the heat regularisation, the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality, as well as the maximal regularity with slow evolution, we obtain a recursive increasing sequence {pj}j=0,1,…\{p_{j}\}_{j=0,1,...} with p0:=1+δ/2p_{0}:=1+\delta/2 satisfying: if

supκ∈(0,∞)2(‖nκ‖L2​pj​(ΩT))≤CT,\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\left(\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2p_{j}}(\Omega_{T})}\right)\leq C_{T},

then

supκ∈(0,∞)2(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκpj+1(t)+∥nκ∥L2​pj+1​(ΩT))≤CT,pj+1,\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p_{j+1}}(t)+\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2p_{j+1}}(\Omega_{T})}\right)\leq C_{T,p_{j+1}},

see Lemma 4.4. This is sufficient to perform a bootstrap argument to have the uniform-in-κ\kappa Lp​(ΩT)L^{p}(\Omega_{T})-boundedness for any 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty that turns into the L∞​(ΩT)L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})-boundedness due to the use of the Neumann heat semigroup. Finally, the convergence rate is obtained similarly to Theorem 1.2 by tracking carefully the dependence of all constants on both ε\varepsilon and τ\tau, as well as the distance from the initial data to the critical manifold 𝒞𝖨𝖣𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{IDS}}, which is defined by

𝒞𝖨𝖣𝖲:={(n,c,w)∈L2​(Ω)×H2​(Ω)×L2​(Ω):(Δ​c−c+w,−w+n)=(0,0)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{IDS}}:=\Big\{(n,c,w)\in L^{2}(\Omega)\times H^{2}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega):\,(\Delta c-c+w,-w+n)=(0,0)\Big\}. (1.47)

The distance distpk,l​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖨𝖣𝖲]\mathrm{dist}^{k,l}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{IDS}}] is defined similarly to (1.32) due to the replacement of 𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}} by 𝒞𝖨𝖣𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{IDS}}.

The case τ=0\tau=0 was investigated in [LX23], where only the convergence of nεn_{\varepsilon} to nn as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 had been showed in a strong sense while cε⇀cc_{\varepsilon}\xrightharpoonup{}c weakly in L4​((0,T),W1,4​(Ω))L^{4}((0,T);W^{1,4}(\Omega)) and weakly-star in L∞​((0,T),H2​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T);H^{2}(\Omega)) and wε⇀ww_{\varepsilon}\xrightharpoonup{}w weakly-star in L∞​(ΩT)L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T}). Our results improve those of [LX23] by proving this convergence in the strong topology, and furthermore provide the convergence rate. Similarly to Corollary 1, we have the following strong convergence to the critical manifold 𝒞𝖨𝖣𝖲\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{IDS}}.

Corollary 2 (Strong convergence to the critical manifold).

For each κ=(ε,τ)∈(0,∞)2\kappa=(\varepsilon,\tau)\in(0,\infty)^{2}, let (nκ,cκ,wκ)(n_{\kappa},c_{\kappa},w_{\kappa}) be the globally classical solution to the system (1)-(1.5). Then,

‖Δ​cκ−cκ+wκ‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖−wκ+nκ‖L2​(ΩT)≤C​|κ|.\displaystyle\|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|-w_{\kappa}+n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C\sqrt{|\kappa|}.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows: In Section 2, we rigorously simplify from (1)-(1.5) to (1.2)-(1.17) in which both subcritical case 1≤N≤31\leq N\leq 3 and critical case N=4N=4 are considered. The accuracy of this simplification is studied in Section 3. In Section 4, the analysis of the indirect-direct simplification from (1)-(1.5) to (1.2), as well as its accuracy, will be investigated. Finally, we place some auxiliary results in the Appendix A.

2 Rigorous parabolic-elliptic simplification

We start this section by the global existence and boundedness of solutions to (1)-(1.5) for fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 and τ>0\tau>0, which is done in [FS17]. We remark that the constant Cε,τC_{\varepsilon,\tau} in the following theorem may tend to infinity as either ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 or τ→0\tau\to 0.

Thanks to the Sobolev embedding, Lemma 2.3 implies that the L6​(Ω)NL^{6}(\Omega)^{N}-norm of ∇v\nabla v is uniformly-in-(ε,t)(\varepsilon,t) bounded. This will help us to obtain the uniform-in-ε\varepsilon boundedness of nεn_{\varepsilon} in

via testing its equation by nεn_{\varepsilon}, see Lemma 2.4. Moreover, in Lemma 2.5, this boundedness of ∇cε\nabla c_{\varepsilon} will show the uniform-in-ε\varepsilon boundedness of nεn_{\varepsilon} in L∞​(ΩT)L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T}) via exploiting Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimates for the Neumann heat semigroup.

Lemma 2.4.

It holds

supε>0(sup0<t<T∫Ωnε2+∬ΩTnε3+∬ΩT|∇nε|2)≤Cτ.\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\left(\sup_{0<t<T}\int_{\Omega}n_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\varepsilon}^{3}+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\right)\leq C_{\tau}. (2.13)

dd​t​∫Ωnε2+∫Ω|∇nε|2≤∫Ωnε2​|∇cε|2,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}n_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\leq\int_{\Omega}n_{\varepsilon}^{2}|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}|^{2},

for all t>0t>0. Then, by the Hölder inequality,

dd​t​∫Ωnε2+∫Ω|∇nε|2≤‖nε‖L3​(Ω)2​‖∇cε‖L6​(Ω)N2.\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}n_{\varepsilon}^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\leq\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{3}(\Omega)}^{2}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{6}(\Omega)^{N}}^{2}. (2.14)

‖nε‖L3​(Ω)2​‖∇cε‖L6​(Ω)N2\displaystyle\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{3}(\Omega)}^{2}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{6}(\Omega)^{N}}^{2} ≤Cτ2​(Cτ​‖∇nε‖L2​(Ω)N4/5​‖nε‖L1​(Ω)1/5+‖nε‖L1​(Ω))2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{2}}\left(\frac{C}{\tau}\|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}\|^{4/5}_{L^{2}(\Omega)^{N}}\|n_{\varepsilon}\|^{1/5}_{L^{1}(\Omega)}+\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\right)^{2},

Lemma 2.5.

For any 0<T<∞0<T<\infty, it holds

for any η>0\eta>0, being chosen later. Using the Hölder inequality,

≤C​‖nε​(s)‖L∞​(Ω)7​p−66​p​‖nε​(s)‖L1​(Ω)6−p6​p​‖∇cε​(s)‖L6​(Ω)N≤Cτ​ΛT7​p−66​p,\displaystyle\leq C\|n_{\varepsilon}(s)\|^{\frac{7p-6}{6p}}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\|n_{\varepsilon}(s)\|^{\frac{6-p}{6p}}_{L^{1}(\Omega)}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(s)\|_{L^{6}(\Omega)^{N}}\leq C_{\tau}\Lambda_{T}^{\frac{7p-6}{6p}},

where supt>0‖∇cε​(t)‖L6​(Ω)N\sup_{t>0}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{6}(\Omega)^{N}} is bounded due to estimate (2.7) and the Sobolev embedding for the dimensions 1≤N≤31\leq N\leq 3. Combining the above estimates, we deduce that

Lemma 2.6.

For any 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, it holds

supε>0(‖wε‖L∞​((0,T),W1,∞​(Ω))+‖Δ​wε‖Lp​(ΩT))≤Cτ,T,\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\Big(\|w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);W^{1,\infty}(\Omega))}+\|\Delta w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}\Big)\leq C_{\tau,T}, (2.15)

≤Cτ​‖w0‖Wk,p2​(Ω)+Cτε|nε|∫0tL∞​((0,T),Lp1​(Ω))⁡e−sε​min​(s/ε,1)−N2​(1p1−1p2)−k2​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq C_{\tau}\|w_{0}\|_{W^{k,p_{2}}(\Omega)}+\frac{C_{\tau}}{\varepsilon}\|n_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{p_{1}}(\Omega))}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\frac{s}{\varepsilon}}\min(s/\varepsilon;1)^{-\frac{N}{2}\big(\frac{1}{p_{1}}-\frac{1}{p_{2}}\big)-\frac{k}{2}}ds

Lemma 2.7.

There exists γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) such that

Recalling for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) is the globally classical solution to (1)-(1.5), so that it is continuous with respect to both time and space variables. Therefore, one can apply [PV93, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4] or [Lan17, Lemma 2.1, Part iv] to claim (2.19), where Cτ,TC_{\tau,T} does not depend on ε\varepsilon due to the uniform boundedness of nεn_{\varepsilon} in Lemma 2.5 and of cεc_{\varepsilon} in Lemma 2.6. ∎

2.2.3 Passage to the limit

Lemma 2.8.

Assume that (n,c,w)(n,c,w) is a globally weak solution to System (1.2)-(1.17) in the sense that

n∈C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])∩L∞​(ΩT)∩L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)),c,w∈L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω)),\displaystyle n\in C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])\cap L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})\cap L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)),\quad c,w\in L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)), (2.20)

and

−∫0T⟨n,∂tξ⟩−∫Ωn0ξ(0)=∬ΩT(−∇n+n∇c)⋅∇ξ,∬ΩT(∇c⋅∇ζ+c​ζ)=∬ΩTw​ζ,∬ΩT(τ∇w⋅∇ζ+wζ)=∬ΩTnζ,\displaystyle\begin{gathered}-\int_{0}^{T}\langle n,\partial_{t}\xi\rangle-\int_{\Omega}n_{0}\xi(0)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(-\nabla n+n\nabla c)\cdot\nabla\xi,\\ \iint_{\Omega_{T}}(\nabla c\cdot\nabla\zeta+c\zeta)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}w\zeta,\\ \iint_{\Omega_{T}}(\tau\nabla w\cdot\nabla\zeta+w\zeta)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n\zeta,\end{gathered}

for all ξ,ζ∈Cc∞​(Ω¯×[0,T))\xi,\zeta\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T)). Then, it is the unique global classical solution to (1.2)-(1.17).

Proof.

We first note that it is straightforward to check the initial condition in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) for nn. Since the weak formulations for cc and ww are standard weak forms of the linear elliptic equations (specifically, the last two equations of (1.2)), it is obvious that they become the strong solutions to

{Δ​c−c+w=0in ​Ω∞,τ​Δ​w−w+n=0in ​Ω∞,∂νc=∂νw=0on ​Γ∞,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllllll}\Delta c-c+w=0&\text{in }\Omega_{\infty},\\ \tau\Delta w-w+n=0&\text{in }\Omega_{\infty},\\ \partial_{\nu}c=\partial_{\nu}w=0&\text{on }\Gamma_{\infty},\end{array}\right.

Using the representation of the inverse operators (−Δ+I)−1(-\Delta+I)^{-1} and (−τ​Δ+I)−1(-\tau\Delta+I)^{-1}, for example, see [RTY24, Appendix B], we have

{c⁡(x,t)=∫0∞es⁡(Δ−I)​w​(x,t)​ds,(x,t)∈Ω¯×[0,T],w⁡(x,t)=∫0∞es⁡(τ​Δ−I)​n​(x,t)​ds,(x,t)∈Ω¯×[0,T].\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}c(x,t)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{s(\Delta-I)}w(x,t)ds,&(x,t)\in\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T],\\ w(x,t)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{s(\tau\Delta-I)}n(x,t)ds,&(x,t)\in\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T].\end{array}\right.

Therefore, the continuity of nn implies the continuity of ww and, then, of cc. Consequently, the Hölder continuity of nn is obtained using the results in [PV93, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4] or in [Lan17, Lemma 2.1, Part iv]. By the representation (2.2.3) again, we claim the Hölder continuity of ww and cc. This allows us to apply [Lan17, Lemma 2.1, Part v] that n∈C2,1​(Ω×(0,T))n\in C^{2,1}(\Omega\times(0,T)), and so (n,c,w)(n,c,w) becomes the unique classical solution to (1.2)-(1.17). ∎

In the following, we present the proof of Theorem 1.1 for setting subcritical dimensions.

Proof of Theorem 1.1 with subcritical dimensions N=1,2,3N=1,2,3.

We first note that boundedness (1.1) has been obtained in Lemmas 2.4, 2.6 and 2.7. In the following, we will prove the convergence of the sequence {(nε,cε,wε)}ε>0\{(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon})\}_{\varepsilon>0} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Thanks to the estimate for nεn_{\varepsilon} in the space of Hölder continuous functions obtained in Lemma 2.7, the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem yields that there exists a subsequence of {nε}ε>0\{n_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0} (being denoted by the same notation) such that

nε⟶n strongly in ​C​(Ω¯×[0,T])\displaystyle n_{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow n\quad\text{ strongly in }C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]) (2.29)

as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Moreover, the estimate for this component in Lemma 2.4 also implies that

∇nε⇀∇n weakly in ​L2​(ΩT).\displaystyle\nabla n_{\varepsilon}\xrightharpoonup{\hskip 11.38092pt}\nabla n\quad\text{ weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}). (2.30)

Testing the equation for nεn_{\varepsilon} by ξ∈Cc∞​(Ω¯×[0,T))\xi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T)), we derive

−∫0T⟨nε,∂tξ⟩−∫Ωn0ξ(0)=∬ΩT(−∇nε+nε∇cε)⋅∇ξ,\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{T}\langle n_{\varepsilon},\partial_{t}\xi\rangle-\int_{\Omega}n_{0}\xi(0)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(-\nabla n_{\varepsilon}+n_{\varepsilon}\nabla c_{\varepsilon})\cdot\nabla\xi,

which, after using the convergence (2.29)-(2.30), shows

−∫0T⟨n,∂tξ⟩−∫Ωn0ξ(0)=∬ΩT(−∇n+n∇c)⋅∇ξ.\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{T}\langle n,\partial_{t}\xi\rangle-\int_{\Omega}n_{0}\xi(0)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(-\nabla n+n\nabla c)\cdot\nabla\xi.

Next, we will consider the limits of cεc_{\varepsilon} and wεw_{\varepsilon}. We note from the previous subsections that the uniform boundedness of ∂tcε\partial_{t}c_{\varepsilon} and ∂twε\partial_{t}w_{\varepsilon} is lacking. Therefore, the compactness of {cε}ε>0\{c_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0} and {wε}ε>0\{w_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0} does not make the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem or the Aubin-Lions lemma applicable. Thanks to Lemma 2.6,

(cε,∇cε)⇀(c,∇c)weakly in ​L2​(ΩT)N+1,(wε,∇wε)⇀(w,∇w)weakly in ​L2​(ΩT)N+1.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lllllll}(c_{\varepsilon},\nabla c_{\varepsilon})&\xrightharpoonup{\hskip 11.38092pt}&(c,\nabla c)&\text{weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T})^{N+1},\\ (w_{\varepsilon},\nabla w_{\varepsilon})&\xrightharpoonup{\hskip 11.38092pt}&(w,\nabla w)&\text{weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T})^{N+1}.\end{array}

Testing the equation for wεw_{\varepsilon} by ζ∈Cc∞​(Ω¯×[0,T))\zeta\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T)) gives

−ε∫Ωwε(0)ζ(0)−ε∬ΩTwε∂tζ+∬ΩT(τ∇wε⋅∇ζ+wεζ)=∬ΩTnεζ.\displaystyle-\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}w_{\varepsilon}(0)\zeta(0)-\varepsilon\iint_{\Omega_{T}}w_{\varepsilon}\partial_{t}\zeta+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(\tau\nabla w_{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla\zeta+w_{\varepsilon}\zeta)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\varepsilon}\zeta. (2.33)

With the boundedness of wεw_{\varepsilon} obtained in Lemma 2.6, we can pass ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 to obtain the weak formulation for ww in (2.8). Note that this can be done similarly for the component cεc_{\varepsilon}. Thus, the limit vector (n,c,w)(n,c,w) is a globally weak solution to System (1.2)-(1.17) in the sense (2.20)-(2.8). Then, Lemma 2.8 yields that this solution becomes the unique globally classical solution of (1.2)-(1.17).

We now improve the convergence of wε,cεw_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon} to a strong sense, which will be basically based on the so-called energy equation method, see e.g. [Bal04, HT16], presented as follows. Recall that

∬ΩT(∇w⋅∇ζ+w​ζ)=∬ΩTn​ζ,for all ​ζ∈Cc∞​(Ω¯×[0,T)),\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(\nabla w\cdot\nabla\zeta+w\zeta)=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n\zeta,\quad\text{for all }\zeta\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T)), (2.34)

and for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, wεw_{\varepsilon} is sufficiently smooth since (nε,cε,wε)(n_{\varepsilon},c_{\varepsilon},w_{\varepsilon}) is the globally classical solution to System (1)-(1.5). Due to an argument of dense spaces, we can choose wεw_{\varepsilon} to be a test function in (2.33), which yields

∬ΩT(|∇wε|2+wε2)=∬ΩTnε​wε−ε2​∫Ω(wε2−w02).\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(|\nabla w_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+w_{\varepsilon}^{2})=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\varepsilon}w_{\varepsilon}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\Omega}(w_{\varepsilon}^{2}-w_{0}^{2}). (2.35)

Then, choosing ξ=w\xi=w in (2.34) gives

∬ΩT(|∇w|2+w2)=∬ΩTn​w,\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(|\nabla w|^{2}+w^{2})=\iint_{\Omega_{T}}nw,

which is combined with (2.35) to show that

|‖wε‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))2−‖w‖L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))2|≤|∬ΩT(nε​wε−n​w)|+ε2​|∫Ω(wε2−w02)|.\displaystyle\left|\|w_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}^{2}-\|w\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}^{2}\right|\leq\left|\iint_{\Omega_{T}}(n_{\varepsilon}w_{\varepsilon}-nw)\right|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\left|\int_{\Omega}(w_{\varepsilon}^{2}-w_{0}^{2})\right|.

Since L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega)) is uniformly convex, this implies

We obtain the convergence stated at (1.23) by collecting (2.29)-(2.30) and (2.36)-(2.37). Since (n,c,w)(n,c,w) is the unique solution to System (1.2)-(1.17), the above convergences hold for the whole sequences. ∎

When N≤3N\leq 3, it is sufficient to use the L1L^{1}-norm of nεn_{\varepsilon} and the embedding H2​(Ω)↪L∞​(Ω)H^{2}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(\Omega) to control the term ∫Ωnε​cε\int_{\Omega}n_{\varepsilon}c_{\varepsilon}. Lemma 2.11.

For 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, it holds that

supε>0(sup0<t<T∫BRnεp​(t)+∬BR×(0,T)|∇nε|2)≤Cp,T.\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\left(\sup_{0<t<T}\int_{B_{R}}n_{\varepsilon}^{p}(t)+\iint_{B_{R}\times(0,T)}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\right)\leq C_{p,T}. (2.44)
Proof.

Using the equation for nεn_{\varepsilon}, one can check that

dd​t​∫BRnεp​(t)=−4​(p−1)p∫BR|∇nεp/2(t)|2+p(p−1)∫BRnεp−1(t)∇nε(t)⋅∇cε(t)≤−4​(p−1)p∫BR|∇nεp/2(t)|2+p⁡(p−1)2∫BRnεp(t)|∇cε(t)|2.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt}\int_{B_{R}}n_{\varepsilon}^{p}(t)&=-\frac{4(p-1)}{p}\int_{B_{R}}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)|^{2}+p(p-1)\int_{B_{R}}n_{\varepsilon}^{p-1}(t)\nabla n_{\varepsilon}(t)\cdot\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\\ &\leq-\frac{4(p-1)}{p}\int_{B_{R}}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)|^{2}+\frac{p(p-1)}{2}\int_{B_{R}}n_{\varepsilon}^{p}(t)|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)|^{2}.\end{aligned} (2.45)

To estimate this energy, we will control the latter term by the product of the integral of nεpn_{\varepsilon}^{p} and a suitable norm of ∇cε\nabla c_{\varepsilon}. Indeed, using the Hölder, the Gagliardo-Nirenberg and the Young inequalities, it can be dealt with as

∫BR(nεp/2​(t))2​|∇cε​(t)|2≤‖nεp/2​(t)‖L83​(BR)2​‖∇cε​(t)‖L8​(BR)2≤(C​‖nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR)12​‖∇nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR)12+C​‖nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR))2​‖∇cε​(t)‖L8​(BR)2≤(C​‖nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR)​‖∇nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR)+C​‖nεp/2​(t)‖L2​(BR)2)​‖∇cε​(t)‖L8​(BR)2≤4p2​∫BR|∇nεp/2​(t)|2+C⁡(p216​‖∇cε​(t)‖L8​(BR)4+‖∇cε​(t)‖L8​(BR)2)​∫BRnεp​(t).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\int_{B_{R}}(n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t))^{2}|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)|^{2}\leq\|n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{\frac{8}{3}}(B_{R})}^{2}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{8}(B_{R})}^{2}\\ &\leq\bigg(C\|n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\|n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\bigg)^{2}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{8}(B_{R})}^{2}\\ &\leq\bigg(C\|n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}\|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}+C\|n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}^{2}\bigg)\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{8}(B_{R})}^{2}\\ &\leq\frac{4}{p^{2}}\int_{B_{R}}|\nabla n_{\varepsilon}^{p/2}(t)|^{2}+C\left(\frac{p^{2}}{16}\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{8}(B_{R})}^{4}+\|\nabla c_{\varepsilon}(t)\|_{L^{8}(B_{R})}^{2}\right)\int_{B_{R}}n^{p}_{\varepsilon}(t).\end{aligned} (2.46)

Thus, we deduce from (2.45) that

(2.47)

It remains to estimate ∇cε\nabla c_{\varepsilon} in L4​((0,T),L8​(BR))L^{4}((0,T);L^{8}(B_{R})), which will be done using Lemmas 2.9-2.10 and A.5. 3 Convergence rates and the initial layer’s effect for PES

In this section, we investigate the accuracy of the parabolic-elliptic simplification presented in Theorem 1.1, with the main result stated in Theorem 1.2. We begin with estimates for the initial layers in Lemma 3.1 and obtain needed regularity for the limiting solution in Lemma 3.2. Then, we present energy estimates for the rate system (1.2) in Lemmas 3.3-3.4, which help us prove Theorem 1.2. Recall that we consider all dimensions 1≤N≤41\leq N\leq 4 in this section.

that

=\displaystyle=\, ∫0∞es⁡(Δ−I)​[−Δ​c0​(x)+c0​(x)−w0​(x)]​𝑑s,\displaystyle\,\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{s(\Delta-I)}[-\Delta c_{0}(x)+c_{0}(x)-w_{0}(x)]ds, (3.3)

and

Let (n,w,c)(n,w,c) be the solution of System (1.2)-(1.17) as obtained in Theorem 1.1. Then

‖∂tw‖L∞​((0,T),L2​(Ω))+‖∂tw‖Lp​(ΩT)+‖∂tc‖L∞​((0,T),H1​(Ω))+‖∂tc‖Lp​(ΩT)≤CT,\displaystyle\|\partial_{t}w\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega))}+\|\partial_{t}w\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}+\|\partial_{t}c\|_{L^{\infty}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))}+\|\partial_{t}c\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C_{T},

(A.2) to obtain the desired estimate for ∂tw\partial_{t}w. The term ∂tc\partial_{t}c is treated similarly using again the representation (3). On the other hand, the boundedness of ∂tc\partial_{t}c and ∂tw\partial_{t}w in Lp​(ΩT)L^{p}(\Omega_{T}) can be obtained directly via the maximal regularity. ∎

≤∫Ωn~εp​(0)+Cp,T​∬Ωtn~εp+Cp,T,τ​(ε2+ε​(dist⁡[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])2).\displaystyle\leq\int_{\Omega}\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}^{p}(0)+C_{p,T}\iint_{\Omega_{t}}\widetilde{n}_{\varepsilon}^{p}+C_{p,T,\tau}\left(\varepsilon^{2}+\varepsilon\big(\mathrm{dist}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)^{2}\right).

(3.11)

Thanks to the boundedness of ∂tc\partial_{t}c, ∂tw\partial_{t}w in Lq​(ΩT)L^{q}(\Omega_{T}) in Lemma 3.2 and the estimate (3.11), we apply the maximal regularity with slow evolution (cf. Lemma A.4) to the equation for w~ε\widetilde{w}_{\varepsilon} that

≤Cp,τ,T​(ε1p​‖−τ​Δ​w0+w0−n0‖W2,p​(Ω)+ε2p+ε1p​(dist⁡[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])2p)\displaystyle\leq C_{p,\tau,T}\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{p}}{\|-\tau\Delta w_{0}+w_{0}-n_{0}\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}}+\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{p}}+\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{p}}\big(\mathrm{dist}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)^{\frac{2}{p}}\right)
≤Cp,τ,T​(ε2p+ε1p​(distp0,2​[(n0,c0,w0);𝒞𝖯𝖤𝖲])2p).\displaystyle\leq C_{p,\tau,T}\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{p}}+\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{p}}\big(\mathrm{dist}^{0,2}_{p}[(n_{0},c_{0},w_{0});\mathcal{C}_{\mathsf{PES}}]\big)^{\frac{2}{p}}\right).

which completes the proof. ∎

4 From indirect signalling to direct signalling

We rigorously study the indirect-direct simplification from (1)-(1.5) to (1.2) in this section. The main result of this part was stated in Theorem 1.3, including both passing to the limit and estimating the convergence rates.

4.1 Balancing the multiple time scale Lyapunov functional

Lemma 4.1.

It holds that

supt>0∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+14​|Δ​cκ−cκ+wκ|2+14​|∇cκ|2+12​cκ2)+1ε∬Ω∞(|∇(Δcκ−cκ+wκ)|2+|Δcκ−cκ+wκ|2)≤C.\displaystyle\begin{gathered}\sup_{t>0}\int_{\Omega}\left(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{1}{4}|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{4}|\nabla c_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{\kappa}^{2}\right)\\ +\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\iint_{\Omega_{\infty}}\Big(|\nabla(\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa})|^{2}+|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}\Big)\leq C.\end{gathered}
Proof.

Similarly to the prooof of Lemma 2.9, we will balance the dissipation inequality in Lemma 2.2. If N=1N=1 then the Sobolev embedding H1​(Ω)↪L∞​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(\Omega) can be utilised to see that

∫Ωnκ​cκ≤‖cκ‖L∞​(Ω)​∫Ωnκ≤C​M​‖cκ‖H1​(Ω)≤14​‖cκ‖H1​(Ω)2+C2​M2.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}c_{\kappa}\leq\|c_{\kappa}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}\leq CM\|c_{\kappa}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{1}{4}\|c_{\kappa}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}^{2}+C^{2}M^{2}.

By skipping the term including τ\tau on the left-hand side of (2.2.1), for all t>0t>0 we get

∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+12​|Δ​cκ−cκ+wκ|2+12​|∇cκ|2+12​cκ2)+1ε∬Ωt(|∇(Δcκ−cκ+wκ)|2+|Δcκ−cκ+wκ|2)≤ℰ⁡(n0,c0)+∫Ωnκ​cκ≤ℰ⁡(n0,c0)+14​‖cκ‖H1​(Ω)2+C.\displaystyle\begin{gathered}\int_{\Omega}\left(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{1}{2}|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla c_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{\kappa}^{2}\right)\\ +\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\iint_{\Omega_{t}}\Big(|\nabla(\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa})|^{2}+|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}\Big)\\ \leq\mathcal{E}(n_{0},c_{0})+\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}c_{\kappa}\leq\mathcal{E}(n_{0},c_{0})+\frac{1}{4}\|c_{\kappa}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}^{2}+C.\end{gathered}

The estimate (4.1) is showed by absorbing the term including ‖cκ‖H1​(Ω)\|c_{\kappa}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} to the left-hand side.

Let us consider N=2N=2 by exploiting the Moser-Trudinger inequality (instead of the Adam type inequality), which is represented in Part a of Lemma A.3. Indeed, for any positive real number α>0\alpha>0 to be chosen later, a combination of the inequalities (A.5) and (A.6) gives

∫Ωnκ​cκ\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}c_{\kappa} ≤1e+1α​∫Ωnκ​log⁡nκ+‖nκ‖L1​(Ω)α​log⁡(∫Ωeα​cκ)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}}{\alpha}\log\left(\int_{\Omega}e^{\,\alpha\,c_{\kappa}}\right)
≤1e+1α​∫Ωnκ​log⁡nκ+Mα​[α28​π​‖∇cκ‖L2​(Ω)2+α|Ω|​∫Ωcκ+Cα]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{M}{\alpha}\left[\frac{\alpha^{2}}{8\pi}\|\nabla c_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}c_{\kappa}+C_{\alpha}\right]
=1α​∫Ωnκ​log⁡nκ+α​M8​π​∫Ω|∇cκ|2+Cα,M,Ω.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{\alpha M}{8\pi}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla c_{\kappa}|^{2}+C_{\alpha,M,\Omega}.

Consequently, it follows from (2.2.1) that

∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+12​|Δ​cκ−cκ+wκ|2+12​|∇cκ|2+12​cκ2)+1ε∬Ωt(|∇(Δcκ−cκ+wκ)|2+|Δcκ−cκ+wκ|2)≤ℰ⁡(n0,c0)+1α​∫Ωnκ​log⁡nκ+α​M8​π​∫Ω|∇cκ|2+C.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\int_{\Omega}\left(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{1}{2}|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla c_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}c_{\kappa}^{2}\right)\\ &+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\iint_{\Omega_{t}}\Big(|\nabla(\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa})|^{2}+|\Delta c_{\kappa}-c_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}|^{2}\Big)\\ &\leq\mathcal{E}(n_{0},c_{0})+\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+\frac{\alpha M}{8\pi}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla c_{\kappa}|^{2}+C.\end{aligned}

Since M<4​πM<4\pi, there always exists α>1\alpha>1 such that α​M/(8​π)<1/2\alpha M/(8\pi)<1/2, which means that the integrals on the latter right-hand side can be controlled by terms on the left-hand side. ∎

Lemma 4.2.

It holds that

supκ∈(0,∞)2(‖nκ‖L2​(ΩT)+‖cκ‖L2​((0,T),H2​(Ω)))≤C.\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\,\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\Big(\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\|c_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}((0,T);H^{2}(\Omega))}\Big)\leq C.
Proof.

By considering the Boltzmann entropy for the first equation of (1), we have

∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+e−1)\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+e^{-1}) =∫Ω(n0​log⁡n0+e−1)−∬Ωt|∇nκ|2nκ−∬Ωtnκ​Δ​cκ\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}(n_{0}\log n_{0}+e^{-1})-{\iint_{\Omega_{t}}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}-{\iint_{\Omega_{t}}}n_{\kappa}\Delta c_{\kappa}
≤C−∬ΩT|∇nκ|2nκ+12​∬ΩTnκ2+12​∬ΩT|Δ​cκ|2,\displaystyle\leq C-\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\Delta c_{\kappa}|^{2},

which shows that

∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+e−1)+∬ΩT|∇nκ|2nκ≤C+12​∬ΩTnκ2+12​∬ΩT|Δ​cκ|2.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+e^{-1})+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}\leq C+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\Delta c_{\kappa}|^{2}.

We will balance the two sides of the above estimate. Thanks to the parabolic maximal regularity with slow evolution (see Lemma A.4) applied to the second equation of System (1),

‖Δ​cκ‖L2​(ΩT)≤C⁡(ε12​‖Δ​c0‖L2​(Ω)+‖wκ‖L2​(ΩT))≤C⁡(ε12​‖Δ​c0‖L2​(Ω)+(ε​∫Ωw02+∬ΩTnκ2)1/2),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \|\Delta c_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}&\leq C\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\Delta c_{0}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\|w_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\right)\\ &\leq C\left(\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\Delta c_{0}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+{\left(\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}w_{0}^{2}+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2}\right)^{1/2}}\right),\end{aligned} (4.3)

where the L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T})-norm of wκw_{\kappa} is controlled by testing the equation for wκw_{\kappa} by wκw_{\kappa}, given as

ε2​∫Ωwκ2+τ​∬ΩT|∇wκ|2+12​∬ΩTwκ2≤ε2​∫Ωw02+12​∬ΩTnκ2.\displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\Omega}w_{\kappa}^{2}+\tau\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla w_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}w_{\kappa}^{2}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\Omega}w_{0}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2}.

Therefore, we obtain

∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+e−1)+∬ΩT|∇nκ|2nκ≤C+C​∬ΩTnκ2.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+e^{-1})+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}\leq C+C\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2}. (4.4)

Due to Lemma 4.1, nκn_{\kappa} is uniformly-in-κ\kappa bounded in L∞​((0,∞),L​log⁡L⁡(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,\infty);L\log L(\Omega)), which suits to apply Lemma A.1 with N≤2N\leq 2 to have that

∬ΩTnκ2\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2} ≤α⁡(supt>0∫Ω(nκ​log⁡nκ+e−1))​∬ΩT|∇nκ|2nκ+Cα​T,\displaystyle\leq\alpha\left(\sup_{t>0}\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}\log n_{\kappa}+e^{-1})\right)\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}+C_{\alpha}T, (4.5)

for any α>0\alpha>0. Consequently,

∬ΩTnκ2\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{2} ≤C​α​∬ΩT|∇nκ|2nκ+Cα​T.\displaystyle\leq C\alpha\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}}{n_{\kappa}}+C_{\alpha}T.

This estimate yields that the L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T})-norm of nκn_{\kappa} in (4.4) can be controlled by the second term on the left-hand side with a sufficiently small α>0\alpha>0. Hence, we obtain the uniform-in-κ\kappa boundedness of |∇nκ|2/nκ|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}/n_{\kappa} in L1​(ΩT)L^{1}(\Omega_{T}), which in a combination with (4.5) concludes that nκn_{\kappa} is uniformly-in-κ\kappa bounded in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}). Then, back to (4.3), we obtain a uniform bound for cκc_{\kappa} in L2​((0,T),H2​(Ω))L^{2}((0,T);H^{2}(\Omega)). ∎

Lemma 4.3.

There is a positive constant δ>0\delta>0 such that

supκ∈(0,∞)2(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκ1+δ2(t)+∥nκ∥L2+δ​(ΩT)+∬ΩTnκδ2−1|∇nκ|2)≤CT.\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{1+\frac{\delta}{2}}(t)+\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2+\delta}(\Omega_{T})}+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{\frac{\delta}{2}-1}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}\right)\leq C_{T}. (4.6)
Proof.

Considering the LpL^{p}-energy functional (with p>1p>1) for the first component of (1),

1p​∫Ωnκp​(t)=−(p−1)∬Ωtnκp−2|∇nκ|2+1p∫Ωn0p+(p−1)∬Ωtnκp−1∇nκ⋅∇cκ=−(p−1)∬Ωtnκp−2|∇nκ|2+1p∫Ωn0p−p−1p∬ΩtnκpΔcκ≤−(p−1)∬Ωtnκp−2|∇nκ|2+1p∫Ωn0p+p−1p​‖nκ‖L2​p​(Ωt)p​‖Δ​cκ‖L2​(Ωt)⏟:=Jκ​(t),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{p}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t)&=-(p-1)\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\int_{\Omega}n_{0}^{p}+(p-1)\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-1}\nabla n_{\kappa}\cdot\nabla c_{\kappa}\\ &=-(p-1)\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\int_{\Omega}n_{0}^{p}-\frac{p-1}{p}\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p}\Delta c_{\kappa}\\ &\leq-(p-1)\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\int_{\Omega}n_{0}^{p}+\underbrace{\frac{p-1}{p}\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2p}(\Omega_{t})}^{p}\|\Delta c_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{t})}}_{:=J_{\kappa}(t)},\end{aligned} (4.7)

in which, we note from Lemma 4.2 that Δ​cκ\Delta c_{\kappa} is uniformly-in-κ\kappa bounded in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}). To balance the LpL^{p}-energy functional, we will estimate the temporal supremum of the integral on the left-hand side, or more precisely, ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(t)\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t). Using the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality of the form

‖f‖L4​(Ω)4≤C​‖∇f‖L2​(Ω)2​‖f‖L2​(Ω)2+C​‖f‖L2​(Ω)4\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}\leq C\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+C\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{4} (4.8)

for f=nκp/2​(s)f=n_{\kappa}^{p/2}(s) (here, s∈(0,t)s\in(0,t)), we get

∫Ωnκ2​p​(s)\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{2p}(s) ≤C​p2​∫Ωnκp−2​(s)​|∇nκ​(s)|2​∫Ωnκp​(s)+C​∫Ωnκp​(s).\displaystyle\leq Cp^{2}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}(s)|\nabla n_{\kappa}(s)|^{2}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s)+C\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s).

Thus, we can estimate

(∬Ωtnκ2​p)12≤(C​p2​ess​sups∈(0,T)​∫Ωnκp​(s)​∬Ωtnκp−2​|∇nκ|2+Ct​ess​sups∈(0,T)​∫Ωnκp​(s))12=Cp(ess​sups∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(s))12(∬Ωtnκp−2|∇nκ|2+Cp2t)12.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \left(\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{2p}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}&\leq\left(Cp^{2}\,\esssup_{s\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s)\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+Ct\esssup_{s\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=Cp\left(\esssup_{s\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{C}{p^{2}}t\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned} (4.9)

≤p−12(∬Ωtnκp−2|∇nκ|2+C​Tp2)+CT(p−1)(ess​sups∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(s)),\displaystyle\leq\frac{p-1}{2}\left(\iint_{\Omega_{t}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}+\frac{CT}{p^{2}}\right)+C_{T}(p-1)\left(\esssup_{s\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(s)\right),

1p∫Ωnκp(t)+p−12∬ΩTnκp−2|∇nκ|2≤CT,p+(p−1)CT(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(t)),\displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t)+\frac{p-1}{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{p-2}|\nabla n_{\kappa}|^{2}\leq C_{T,\,p}+(p-1)C_{T}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t)\right), (4.10)

1p(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(t))≤CT,p+CT(p−1)(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκp(t)).\displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t)\right)\leq C_{T,\,p}+C_{T}(p-1)\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p}(t)\right).

p0>1andpj+1:=pj+δ/2​ for ​j=0,1,…p_{0}>1\quad\text{and}\quad p_{j+1}:=p_{j}+\delta/2\text{ for }j=0,1,\dots

then

supκ∈(0,∞)2(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκpj+1(t)+∥nκ∥L2​pj+1​(ΩT))≤CT,pj+1.\displaystyle\sup_{\kappa\in(0,\infty)^{2}}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p_{j+1}}(t)+\|n_{\kappa}\|_{L^{2p_{j+1}}(\Omega_{T})}\right)\leq C_{T,p_{j+1}}. (4.12)

The main idea of this proof is to balance the Lpj+1L^{p_{j+1}}-energy estimate from the L2​pj​(ΩT)L^{2p_{j}}(\Omega_{T})-regularity given in the assumption (4.11). Taking p=pj+1p=p_{j+1} in the energy estimate (4.7), we have

First, let us show that Δ​cκ\Delta c_{\kappa} is uniformly-in-κ\kappa bounded in L2​pj​(ΩT)L^{2p_{j}}(\Omega_{T}), based on the assumption (4.11). Indeed, the parabolic maximal regularity with slow evolution (see Lemma A.4) yields

≤CT,pj+1,η+ηCpj+1(ess​supt∈(0,T)∫Ωnκpj+1(t)+∬ΩTnκpj+1−2(s)|∇nκ(s)|2+CT).\displaystyle\leq C_{T,\,p_{j+1},\eta}+\eta C_{p_{j+1}}\left(\esssup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}n_{\kappa}^{p_{j+1}}(t)+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}n_{\kappa}^{p_{j+1}-2}(s)|\nabla n_{\kappa}(s)|^{2}+CT\right).

4.2 Passage to the limit and convergence rate analysis

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Based on the uniform-in-κ\kappa regularity obtained in Lemma 4.5, one can adapt all steps from the proof of Theorem 1.1 to prove the passage to the limit given in this theorem. For the convergence rate estimates, the estimate (3.10) still holds, i.e.,

dd​t​∫Ω[(nκ​(t)−n⁡(t))2+ε⁡(CT2​(cκ​(t)−c⁡(t)) 2+CT​(wκ​(t)−w⁡(t))2)]+∫Ω|∇(nκ​(t)−n⁡(t))|2\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\left[(n_{\kappa}(t)-n(t))^{2}+\varepsilon\left(\frac{C_{T}}{2}(c_{\kappa}(t)-c(t))^{\,2}+C_{T}(w_{\kappa}(t)-w(t))^{2}\right)\right]+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla(n_{\kappa}(t)-n(t))|^{2}
≤3​CT​∫Ω(nκ​(t)−n⁡(t))2+CT​ε2​∫Ω|∂tc|2+2​CT​ε2​∫Ω|∂tw|2,\displaystyle\leq 3C_{T}\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}(t)-n(t))^{2}+C_{T}\varepsilon^{2}\int_{\Omega}|\partial_{t}c|^{2}+2C_{T}\varepsilon^{2}\int_{\Omega}|\partial_{t}w|^{2},

since ∇cκ\nabla c_{\kappa} is uniformly-in-κ\kappa bounded in L∞​(ΩT)NL^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})^{N} as Lemma 4.5, which consequently shows (1.53). On the other hand, by skipping the term including τ\tau at the estimate (3.6), and then using the comparison principle for differential equations in Lemma A.6, we get (1.54). The estimate (1.55) is obtained similarly to the rest of the proof of Theorem 1.2. ∎

It remains to prove Corollary 2.

=\displaystyle=\, ε​∫Ω(nκ​(T)​wκ​(T)−n0​wκ​(0))−ε​∬ΩTwκ​∂tnκ\displaystyle\,\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}(T)w_{\kappa}(T)-n_{0}w_{\kappa}(0))-\varepsilon\iint_{\Omega_{T}}w_{\kappa}\partial_{t}n_{\kappa}
−\displaystyle-\, ∬ΩT(τ​nκ​Δ​wκ+wκ​(ε​∂twκ−τ​Δ​wκ))\displaystyle\,\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\big(\tau n_{\kappa}\Delta w_{\kappa}+w_{\kappa}(\varepsilon\partial_{t}w_{\kappa}-\tau\Delta w_{\kappa})\big)
=\displaystyle=\, ε∫Ω(nκ(T)wκ(T)−n0wκ(0))+ε∬ΩT(∇nκ⋅∇wκ−nκ∇cκ⋅∇wκ)\displaystyle\,\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}(n_{\kappa}(T)w_{\kappa}(T)-n_{0}w_{\kappa}(0))+\varepsilon\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\big(\nabla n_{\kappa}\cdot\nabla w_{\kappa}-n_{\kappa}\nabla c_{\kappa}\cdot\nabla w_{\kappa}\big)
+\displaystyle+\, τ​∬ΩT(∇nκ⋅∇wκ−|∇wκ|2)−ε2​∫Ω(wκ2​(T)−wκ2​(0)),\displaystyle\,\tau\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\big(\nabla n_{\kappa}\cdot\nabla w_{\kappa}-|\nabla w_{\kappa}|^{2})-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\Omega}(w_{\kappa}^{2}(T)-w_{\kappa}^{2}(0)),
